The order of blocks was counterbalanced across participants. On
each trial, a fixation cross appeared for 1,000 ms. This was then
replaced by the digit, which remained onscreen for either 1,500 ms
or until the participant had made a response. This was followed by
a blank screen for 1,000 ms before the fixation point for the next
trial. The experimental session consisted of two blocks of 96 trials
each, with 12 presentations of each number in both blocks (total
192 trials). Each experimental block was preceded by a practice
block of 24 trials.

with a direct path from inequality beliefs) would predict weaker inten-

path model including both dummy variables as predictors and the hy-
pothesized pathways. We allowed the error terms between the
dummy variables as well as anger and efﬁcacy to co-vary in all models.
Satisfactory ﬁt is indicated by a non-signiﬁcant χ2, the Comparative Fit
Index (CFI) ≥0.95, and the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation
(RSMEA) ≤0.06 (Hu & Bentler, 1999).
Our hypothesized model ﬁt the data very well, χ2(6) = 4.58, p =
.598, CFI = 1.00, and RMSEA = 0.00. Path analyses of the hypothesized
model further showed that both efﬁcacy and anger were signiﬁcant
predictors of collective action intentions, and recognition of differences,
in turn, was a signiﬁcant predictor of both anger and group-efﬁcacy be-
liefs. We then calculated the indirect effects in the path model, and
95% bias corrected conﬁdence intervals, based on 10,000 resamples.
In line with our predictions, the indirect effects for Dummy 1 through
